By extracting the G-Man from a literal "sci-fi villain" context and looking at him through this corporate lens, his operation can be formalized as follows: 
1. The G-Man as a Foresight & Strategy Consultant
In financial and macroeconomic consulting, a foresight specialist doesn't predict a single static future; instead, they map out multiple probabilistic branches (scenarios). 
  • The "Employers" as Shareholders: The G-Man’s unseen employers represent an institutional board of directors or an asset management firm (0:31). They have structural interests in the "macroeconomy" of the multiverse (11:47). 
  • The "Assets" as Investments: Characters like Gordon Freeman and Alyx Vance are not heroes to the G-Man; they are highly leveraged risk-mitigation assets (0:50). He buys them low, puts them in stasis (capital preservation), and deploys them into volatile markets (events like the Black Mesa incident or the Combine occupation) to force a structural shift (2:54).

2. "Nudging" as Pure Behavioral Economics
In real-world economics, a "Nudge" (coined by Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein) is a subtle intervention in the "choice architecture" that predictably alters people's behavior without forbidding any options or significantly changing their economic incentives. 
  • Avoiding Direct Force: The G-Man explicitly notes that completely removing the Combine from Earth would require a "considerably large nudge" that conflicts with the portfolio interests of his employers (11:47). Direct warfare or complete eradication is too expensive and disrupts the market. 
  • Game Theory Without the Video Game: Instead of rewriting reality or using brute force, he alters minor variables—placing the right man in the wrong place (4:42), or providing a specific piece of information (e.g., whispering "prepare for unforeseen consequences" (10:26)). By slightly altering the architecture of choice, he forces human actors and the Combine to react dynamically, changing the long-term timeline through their own autonomous decisions. 
3. The Structural Cost of a "Large Nudge"
When Alyx asks for a massive correction (the Combine off Earth) (11:47), the G-Man rejects it from a purely financial and transactional standpoint. In corporate game theory, a massive, unhedged intervention carries a catastrophic risk of unintended cascading externalities across the rest of their portfolio.
